zedificare.c: ZEDIFICARE Lat. In civil and old English law. To make or build a house; to erect a building. Dig. 45, 1, 75, 7. Adiflcare in tuo proprio solo non licet quod alteri noceat. 3 Inst. 201. To build upon your own land what may injure another is not lawful. A proprietor of land has no right to erect an edifice on his own ground, interfering with the duo enjoyment ZEDIFICATUM of adjoining premises, as by overhanging them, or by throwing water from the roof and eaves upon them, or by obstructing ancient lights and windows. Broom, Max. 869. Ædificatum solo solo cedit. What is built upon land belongs to or goes with land. Broom, Max. 172; Co. Litt. 4a. Ædificia solo cedunt. Buildings belong to [go with]the soil. Fleta, lib. 8, c. 2, § 12.

zedilitumedictum.c: ZEDILITUM EDICTUM Inthe Roman law. The Adilitian Edict; an edict providing remedies for frauds in sales, the execution of which belonged to the curule ediles. Dig. 21, 1. See Cod. 4, 58. ÆFESN. In old English law. The remuneration to the proprietor of a domain for the privilege of feeding swine under the oaks and beeches of his woods. ÆGROTO. Lat. Being sick or indisposed. A term used in some of the older reports. Holt egroto.” 11 Mod. 179.

zegylde.c: ZEGYLDE Uncompensated, unpaid for, unavenged. From the participle of exclusion, G, @, or ex, (Goth.,) and gild, payment, requital. Anc. Inst. Eng. ÆL. A Norman French term signifying “grandfather.” It is also spelled “aieul” and “ayle.” Kelham. Aquior est dispositio legis quam hominis. The disposition of the law is more equitable than that of man. 8 Coke, 152. ÆQUITAS. In the civil law. Equity, as opposed to strictum or summum jus, (q. v.) Otherwise called equum, equum bonum, equim et bonum, equum et justum. Calvin. Aquitas agit in personam. Equity 4 Bouv. Inst. n. 3733. Equitas est correctio legis generaliter lates, qua parte deficit. Equity is the correction of that wherein the law, by reason of its generality, is delicient. Plowd. 375. Æquitas est correctio quædam legi adhibita, quia ab e abest aliquid propter generalem sine exceptione comprehenacts upon the person. 47 A SUUM sionem. Equity is a certain correction applied to law, because on account of its general comprehensiveness, without an exception, something is absent from it. Plowd. 467. Aquitas est perfecta queedam ratio quee jus scriptum interpretatur et emendat; nulla scriptura comprehensa, sed solum in ver ratione consistens. Equity is a certain perfect reason, which interprets and amends the written law, comprehended in no writing, but consisting in right reason alone. Co. Litt. 24b. Æquitas est quasi æqualitas. Equity is as it were equality; equity is a species of equality or equalization. Co. Litt. 24. Aquitas ignorantis opitulatur, oscitantis non item. Equity assists ignorance, but not carelessness, ASquitas non facit jus, sed juri auxiliatur. Equity does not make law, but assists law. Lofft, 379. Equitas nunquam contravenit leges. Equity never counteracts the laws. Equitas sequitur legem. lows the law. Gilb. 186. Equitas supervacua odit. Equity abhors superfluous things. Lofft, 282. Æquitas uxoribus, liberis, creditoribus maxime favet. Equity favors wives and children, creditors most of all. Æquum et bonum est lex legum. What is equitable and good is the law of laws. Hob. 224. ÆRA, or ERA. A fixed point of chronological time, whence any number of years is counted; thus, the Christian era began at the birth of Christ, and the Mohammedan era at the flight of Mohammed from Mecca to Medina. The derivation of the word has been much contested. Wharton. ÆRARIUM. Lat. In the Roman law. The treasury, (fiscus.) Calvin. ÆS. Lat. In the Roman law. Money, literally, brass;) metallic money in general, including gold. Dig. 9, 2, 2, pr.; Id. 9, 2. 27, 5; Id. 50, 16, 159. ÆS ALIENUM. zesnecia.c: ZESNECIA Jn old English law. Esnecy; the right or privilege of the eldest born. Spelman; Glanv. lib. 7, c. 3; Fleta, lib. 2, c. 66, $$ 5, 6.

zestimatiocapitis.c: ZESTIMATIO CAPITIS In Saxon law. The estimation or valuation of the head; the price or value of a man. By the laws of Athelstan, the life of every man, not excepting that of the king himself, was estimated at a certain price, which was called the were, or @stimatio capitis. Crabb, Eng. Law, c. 4. Æstimatio preteriti delicti ex postremo facto nunquam crescit. The weight of a past offense is never increased by a subsequent fact. Bacon. TAS INFANTIÆ PROXIMA. In the civil law. The age next to infancy; the first half of the period of childhood, (pueritia,) extending from seven years to ten and a half. Inst. 3, 20, 9; 4 BI. Comm. 22.

zant.c: ZANT Anancient coin, first issued at Constantinople; it was of two sorts,—gold, equivalent to a ducat, valued at 9s. 6d.; and silver, computed at 23. They were both current in England. Wharton.

zeailot.c: ZEAIL OT This word is commonly taken in a bad sense, as denoting a separatist from the Church of England, orafanatic. Brown.

zealouswitness.c: ZEALOUS WITNESS An untechnical term denoting a witness, on the trial of a cause, who manifests a partiality for the side calling him, and an eager readiness to tell anything which he thinks may be of advantage to that side.

zeir.c: ZEIR O. Sc. Year. “Zeir and day Bell.

zemindar.c: ZEMINDAR In Hindu law. Landkeeper. An officer who under the Mohammedan government was charged with the financia. superintendence of the lands of a district, the protection of the cultivators, and the realization of the government’s share of its produce, either in money or Kind. Wharton.

zigari.c: ZIGARI or ZINGARI. Rogues and vagabonds in the middle ages; from Zigi, now Circassia. ee’

zollverein.c: ZOLL-VEREIN A union of German states for uniformity of customs, established in 1819. It continued until the unification of the German empire, including Prussia, Saxony, Bavaria, Wurtemberg, Baden, Hesse-Cassel, Brunswick, and Mecklenburg- Strelitz, and all intermediate principalities. It has now been superseded by the German empire; and the federal council of the empire has taken the place of that of the Zoll-Verein. Wharton.

zygocephalum.c: ZYGOCEPHALUM In the civil law. A measure or quantity of land. Nov. 17, c. 8. As much land as a yoke of oxen could plow in aday. Calvin.

zygostates.c: ZYGOSTATES In the civil law. A weigher; an otħcer who held or looked to the balance in weighing money between buyer and seller; an offer appointed to determine controversies about the weight of money. Spelman.
